title: Should You Buy Hewlett Packard Enterprise Stock For Its Cash?
detail:
Should You Buy Hewlett Packard Enterprise Stock For Its Cash?
Trefis Team

Trading disclosure
Image from Pixabay

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise (HPE) produced free cash flow equal to 5.6% of its market value over the past year, against 4.3% for the median S&P 500 company. A yield that high marks either a business on sale or one the market expects to shrink, and the price appears to assume HPE's server and networking sales will not keep producing this much cash. So how much of that cash can you count on?

HPE's Cash Is At A Three-Year High

HPE has produced free cash in every twelve-month period since mid-2023, but only the past year brought this much. The total reached $4.16 billion, against $0.225 billion in the twelve months before. After lenders are served, that cash belongs to owners whether or not HPE pays it out. If the market comes to give that cash more credit, the share price could rise to reflect it.

The cash comes from a bigger business. Revenue reached $41.9 billion over the past year, up 26.6%. That period includes the Juniper Networks business HPE bought. In the latest quarter, management said orders were led by demand in traditional servers, AI systems, and networking. HPE spent 37.9% of the cash its operations brought in on capital spending.

Part of the cash must serve lenders first. HPE's debt minus its cash came to $14.0 billion at the end of July 2026, or 18.9% of its market value. Against market value plus that debt, the yield is 4.7%. After selling its Telco Solutions business, management said on its September 2, 2026 call that it would retire $1.25 billion of notes maturing that month.

Management Expects Thinner Margins As AI Sales Grow

HPE already earns a thin profit on each sale. Its operating margin was 7.8% over the past year, against 18.5% for the S&P 500 taken as one company. That margin has risen from 6.2% the year before.

Management expects some near-term pressure on that profit. On its September 2 call, management said gross margin should move back toward historical levels as AI systems grow and traditional server prices normalize, and the operating margin should fall in fiscal Q4 2026 on a higher mix of AI systems and on pricing. Both are forecasts, not reported falls. Shortages of parts, DDR5 among them, have also limited how many traditional servers HPE can ship, management said.

Management is working on margins and supply. It expects $600 million a year of savings from the Juniper Networks acquisition by the end of fiscal 2028, and the company is seeking multiyear supply agreements with its partners. It also raised its fiscal 2027 revenue growth forecast to 15% at the midpoint, from 10%. So the doubt is about how much HPE keeps from each sale, not about a business that is shrinking.

title: Will Super Micro (SMCI) Beat Estimates Again in Its Next Earnings Report?
detail:
Will Super Micro (SMCI) Beat Estimates Again in Its Next Earnings Report?
Zacks Equity Research
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 8:10 AM PDT 3 min read
SMCI
Trade SMCI on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Looking for a stock that has been consistently beating earnings estimates and might be well positioned to keep the streak alive in its next quarterly report? Super Micro Computer (SMCI), which belongs to the Zacks Computer- Storage Devices industry, could be a great candidate to consider.

This server technology company has an established record of topping earnings estimates, especially when looking at the previous two reports. The company boasts an average surprise for the past two quarters of 91.67%.

For the last reported quarter, Super Micro came out with earnings of $1.7 per share versus the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $0.68 per share, representing a surprise of 150.00%. For the previous quarter, the company was expected to post earnings of $0.63 per share and it actually produced earnings of $0.84 per share, delivering a surprise of 33.33%.

Price and EPS Surprise

With this earnings history in mind, recent estimates have been moving higher for Super Micro. In fact, the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction) for the company is positive, which is a great sign of an earnings beat, especially when you combine this metric with its nice Zacks Rank.

Our research shows that stocks with the combination of a positive Earnings ESP and a Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) or better produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time. In other words, if you have 10 stocks with this combination, the number of stocks that beat the consensus estimate could be as high as seven.

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Super Micro currently has an Earnings ESP of +36.36%, which suggests that analysts have recently become bullish on the company's earnings prospects. This positive Earnings ESP when combined with the stock's Zacks Rank #3 (Hold) indicates that another beat is possibly around the corner. We expect the company's next earnings report to be released on November 3, 2026.

Investors should note, however, that a negative Earnings ESP reading is not indicative of an earnings miss, but a negative value does reduce the predictive power of this metric.

Many companies end up beating the consensus EPS estimate, though this is not the only reason why their shares gain. Additionally, some stocks may remain stable even if they end up missing the consensus estimate.

Super Micro Computer (SMCI) stock is back in focus after the artificial intelligence (AI) server maker delivered a major boost to its fiscal first-quarter revenue outlook, providing investors with a fresh reason to revisit the stock. Supermicro raised its Q1 fiscal 2027 revenue guidance to $18.5 billion-$19.5 billion from its previous forecast of $14.5 billion-$15.5 billion. At the midpoint, the new outlook is about $4 billion higher than the previous guidance, underscoring the strength of demand for AI infrastructure.

The upbeat preliminary update also included a significant improvement in the company's gross margin outlook, which was raised to 12%-12.5% from 10.4%-10.8%, primarily due to a more favorable customer and product mix. title: If I Could Only Buy 1 AI Stock in November After This Sell-Off, It Would Be This One.

If I Could Only Buy 1 AI Stock in November After This Sell-Off, It Would Be This One.
Micah Zimmerman, The Motley Fool

Last week, the artificial intelligence trade had its roughest week in months, and it was not just one company's problem. A hot inflation report raised the odds that borrowing costs will stay expensive, Goldman Sachs (NYSE: GS) and its CEO warned about debt piling up behind data center build-outs, and the selling spread quickly.

Oracle fell about 9%. Advanced Micro Devices dropped a similar amount. Super Micro Computer lost 23% and was the worst stock in the S&P 500. Palantir Technologies slid into correction territory as AI software names shed roughly $260 billion in value. CoreWeave and its $50 billion in debt made the headlines, but the damage extended to companies with no debt at all.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

That is where the opportunity is.

Image source: Getty Images.
Why Astera Labs got caught in the AI sell-off

Astera Labs (NASDAQ: ALAB) fell over 15% last week, and nothing about its business changed. The company makes the connectivity chips that sit between GPUs, CPUs, and memory inside AI servers, the retimers, switches, and cable modules that keep signals clean as data moves faster. If you think of a GPU as the engine, Astera makes the wiring harness. When investors dump anything tied to data center spending, Astera goes with it, even though it has no borrowings and about $1.25 billion in cash and short-term investments.

The sell-off was about who can afford to keep building. Astera is not the one borrowing.

What Astera Labs did this fall while the market panicked

The reason to buy this dip rather than any other one is what the company shipped in the weeks around it. On Oct. 8, Astera announced Aries 7, which it calls the industry's first full lineup of PCIe 7 signal-conditioning chips spanning both copper and optical links. PCIe 7 is the next-generation standard for moving data between chips, and Astera's parts now cover everything from a few centimeters of circuit board to more than 50 meters of fiber between racks. Intel and AMD, which have both validated Astera's retimers since PCIe 4, are collaborating with the company on the PCIe 7 transition. Samples ship this quarter.

Four days later, at the Open Compute Project summit, Astera unveiled Orion, a rack-scale reference design that lets a cloud provider pick whichever GPU or CPU is cheapest or most available and swap it later without redesigning the rack. It scales to 160 accelerators per pod and is built for neoclouds and enterprises serving AI inference.

SMCI has crashed 61% since VOO and other S&P 500 index funds were forced to buy it at $90.55, a price they had no choice but to accept.

Switching from VOO to IVV changes nothing because both track the same index and follow the identical inclusion buying schedule.

VOO holds 519 stocks across $1.675 trillion in assets, so one bad inclusion is a rounding error. That calculus changes when a hot stock joins at significant weight.

On March 1, 2024, the day its addition to the S&P 500 was announced, Super Micro Computer (NASDAQ:SMCI) closed at a split-adjusted $90.55. As of October 21, 2026, it traded at $35.44. From that announcement close, the dividend-adjusted price change is -60.86%. If you own Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:VOO), your fund had to buy the stock anyway.

bigjom jom / Shutterstock.com

Look at the headlines from that day. CNBC wrote that Super Micro was joining the index after its price soared more than twentyfold in two years. Reuters reported that the shares surged on the news. The stock was announced for inclusion on March 1 and entered the index soon thereafter. The figures in this article all start from the announcement date, not from Super Micro's first day inside the index.

Your Fund's Rulebook Buys Stocks Without Judging the Price

Vanguard's April 28, 2026 prospectus spells out the mechanism clearly. The fund "attempts to replicate the Target Index by investing all, or substantially all, of its assets in the stocks that make up the Target Index, holding each stock in approximately the same proportion as its weighting in the Target Index."

Read that as a rule, because that is how the fund works. The announcement moves the price. Then the fund purchases after the news that raised the stock is already public. Index funds are price-takers (buyers who accept any price) at inclusion. They have no option to wait for a better entry.
